summary: US trade adviser Robert Lighthizer urged tougher rules of origin in the scheduled review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, aiming to narrow the US trade deficit with Mexico. The push comes as Mexico's share of US steel imports fell to 9% from 11% under Section 232 tariffs, adding pressure on Mexico ahead of the 2026 negotiation. Separately, Pemex and Petrobras are studying deepwater and pre-salt assets in the Gulf of Mexico to reduce exploration risk.

lead.h1: US trade adviser Robert Lighthizer urges tougher rules of origin in review of the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement
lead.context: Lighthizer says the scheduled review of the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement should include stricter rules of origin to narrow the US trade deficit with Mexico, an early sign of the tougher terms Washington may seek in the 2026 negotiation.
lead.background: The US-Mexico-Canada Agreement's Article 34.7 now requires the United States, Mexico and Canada to review the trade pact annually, after Washington declined a 16-year extension in July 2026. Rules of origin set how much regional, and how much Chinese, content a product can contain and still qualify for tariff-free treatment.
lead.view: Lighthizer no longer holds office, but as the pact's original architect his push for tighter rules of origin signals the pressure Mexico can expect. Mexico imported $129.5bn in goods from China in 2024 against $9.1bn in exports there, and stricter content rules would force manufacturers to swap suppliers or lose tariff-free access, raising costs across the $872bn US-Mexico trade relationship.
lead.prediction: Rules of origin are likely to dominate the 2026 review without an immediate treaty change, since annual reviews do not require renegotiation. That would be wrong if the three countries agree on revised origin language or a country moves toward withdrawal this cycle.

items.headline: Mexico's share of US steel imports falls to 9% amid tariff changes
items.context: Mexico's share of US steel article imports dropped from 11% as Section 232 tariffs reshaped sourcing, adding pressure on Mexico's push for tariff relief and stricter regional content rules in the review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
items.background: Section 232 tariffs let the United States impose duties on imported steel and aluminum for national-security reasons, applied separately from US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement preferences. Mexico's steel exports to the United States compete with other suppliers whose market access shifts as those tariffs change.
items.view: Mexico's steel share of US imports fell two percentage points, from 11% to 9%, even while it remains inside a preferential trade agreement, showing that US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement membership does not shield exporters from tariffs applied at the border. The loss adds pressure on Mexican negotiators, who are seeking a steel tariff exemption in the same review where Washington is pushing stricter rules of origin.
items.prediction: Mexico is likely to keep pressing for a steel tariff carve-out during the ongoing review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement without a near-term resolution, since tariff and rules-of-origin issues are being negotiated together. That expectation would be wrong if the United States grants Mexico a specific steel exemption before the review concludes.

items.headline: Pemex and Petrobras study deepwater and pre-salt assets in the Gulf of Mexico
items.context: The state oil companies aim to reduce exploration risk and open new opportunities in Pemex's offshore portfolio through technical cooperation.
items.background: Pemex has struggled with deepwater exploration because it lacks the technical experience Petrobras built in Brazil's pre-salt fields, one of the most complex offshore plays in the world.
items.view: Sharing seismic data and exploration methods is a low-cost way for Pemex to reduce risk on projects it could not otherwise justify funding alone. This is a technical cooperation agreement, not a joint venture or capital commitment, so it does not address Pemex's financing gap or change the money the government spends propping up the company. Any output from these eight offshore assets is years away even under a favorable outcome.
items.prediction: Pemex and Petrobras are likely to spend months to years on data review before any drilling decision follows. That view would be wrong if either company announces a capital commitment or a specific well to be drilled rather than continued study.
